source.title: Dimension-adapted Momentum Outscales SGD
source.authors: Damien Ferbach; Katie Everett; Gauthier Gidel; Elliot Paquette; Courtney Paquette

record.file_problem: The supplied text is cut off at 400,000 characters, partway through Appendix L. The main paper and most appendices are present; later material is missing.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures loss scaling and compute-optimal allocations, but changes the optimizer and studies a random-features model plus LSTMs rather than reproducing the original scaling-law experiments.
record.gate_note: The paper's own PLRF analyses and experiments and its LSTM language-model results are included. Results attributed only to cited work, including the original Kaplan and Hoffmann findings, are not rows. The paper reports PLRF experiments over 84 (α, β) pairs, but most results are summarized by regimes rather than separately for every pair.
record.test_reason: Most of the paper is theory and simulation on a synthetic power-law random-features (PLRF) regression model, which is not a language model, so those results bear on no version. The part that tests the claim is a new setting: 2-layer LSTMs trained on C4 next-token prediction. There the authors fit compute-optimal validation-loss frontiers (Chinchilla Approach 1) and report power-law fits with R² ≥ 0.984. They also show the fitted exponent moves with the optimizer and its momentum schedule (κ3). That bears on V1 (power law in compute) and V7 (exponent depends on training choices). No parameter or data allocation exponent is reported for the LSTMs, so V3 is not tested in a language model.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that DANA outscales SGD on PLRF for 2α > 1 by scaling Nesterov-type momentum with dimension and data. Constant momentum (SGD-M), Schedule-Free SGD, and apparently Adam with cosine decay keep SGD's exponents. PLRF works as a proxy for LSTMs, where DANA improves the loss exponent for κ3 between 0.6 and 0.9. They add that α's meaning in LSTMs is unclear and that cross-entropy theory and adaptive methods are left to future work.
record.recipe_differences: This study analyzes optimizer-dependent scaling in a power-law random-features model and tests momentum schedules on C4-trained LSTMs; it does not reproduce the original large-language-model parameter/token/compute sweeps.
record.method_sensitivity: Loss exponents and compute-optimal allocations depend on optimizer and (α, β) phase. LSTM loss behavior varies with the DANA-decaying exponent κ3. Fitted exponents are sensitive to the selected FLOPs window, which the authors manually adjusted.

fits_no_version.finding: On the PLRF model, loss is a sum of power laws in iterations and parameters, and dimension-adapted momentum (DANA) raises the loss exponents above SGD's for 2α > 1. Constant momentum (SGD-M) gives SGD's exponents.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In solvable random-features models, scaling-law exponents can be changed by dimension-dependent optimizer hyperparameters.

fits_no_version.finding: On PLRF, compute-optimal exponents depend on optimizer and phase. DANA-decaying is never compute-optimal at d⋆ ≍ f^(1/2) for 2α > 1. Theory matches experiment within 0.09 (loss) and 0.13 (parameters). Fitted exponents are sensitive to the FLOPs window used.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Compute-optimal allocation in proxy models depends on the optimizer, and Approach 1 exponent fits depend on the fitting window.

record.problems: The main theory is for a quadratic synthetic PLRF model and relies on simplified ODEs; the paper itself says that a full convergence argument beyond quadratics and cross-entropy theory would be desirable. LSTM results use a particular 2-layer architecture and C4, and the authors say α is not clearly defined in that setting. Scaling-exponent fits use manually chosen FLOPs windows and are reported as sensitive to that choice. Stochastic runs use 10 seeds in most PLRF experiments and 100 when β ≤ 0.3, but no standard deviations or confidence intervals are reported in the supplied text.
record.rows_left_out: The paper reports PLRF sweeps over 84 (α, β) pairs and many model sizes, plus LSTM sweeps over 13 embedding sizes and many κ3 values. These are not expanded into separate rows for every pair, size, or κ3 because the supplied text generally summarizes the results by phase or range and does not give separate numeric outcomes for each. Additional individual curves are in Figures 18–21 and 24–41, and detailed experimental material is in Appendices K and L.

untested.parts: Transformer LMs. Separate power laws in parameters and in tokens. Scaling beyond the intermediate LSTM sizes.
Entire version: no small-to-large extrapolation test.
No compute-optimal parameter or token exponent is reported for the LSTM language models. Allocation results exist only for PLRF.
Entire version: depth is fixed at 2 and embedding and hidden sizes are co-scaled.
Parameter counting, data, and fitting-method effects in LMs. The FLOPs-window sensitivity is reported only for PLRF.

missing.what: SGD-M matches SGD's loss exponent on the LSTMs, i.e. a training choice that does not shift the exponent (V7).
Per-κ3 LSTM compute-optimal loss exponents across the full sweep, with R² ≥ 0.984. Numbers appear only in the figure.
Authors state the power-law compute-optimal regime holds only on intermediate model sizes, implying bending at the ends.

record.verdict_notes: PLRF rows were unlinked because the versions concern language-model scaling. The reader's V3 verdicts rested entirely on PLRF and are withdrawn. The LSTM exponent gap is small (0.004); no uncertainty is reported for it, so the outscaling magnitude should be read cautiously. The text was cut off partway through Appendix L.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test large transformer language models or establish separate independent sweeps of parameters, tokens, and compute with the other quantities explicitly held non-bottlenecked.

No fits on small runs are used to predict the loss of runs orders of magnitude larger. Agreement between the paper's ODE predictions and experiments is not a small-run-to-large-run extrapolation test.
Compute-optimal allocations are derived and tested for PLRF, not for large language models. The LSTM experiments do not report separate fitted exponents for optimal parameter count and token count.
No controlled comparison varies depth, width, or other architecture features while holding parameter count fixed.
The study does not test other modalities, repeated-data training, fine-tuning, or transfer. Its LSTM experiment is text next-token training.

The study examines optimizer choice and sensitivity to the FLOPs window used for fitting, but does not compare parameter-counting conventions or systematically vary data and training schedule while refitting the same runs.

rows.subject: PLRF (power law random features model)
rows.stage_stated: one-pass stochastic training on synthetic data
rows.operation_detail: Analyzed and measured population loss over iteration count and parameter dimension for SGD and SGD-M.

conditions.value: varies with (α, β); four distinct loss-curve phases

rows.measure: Population loss P(t; d) and its power-law components in iterations t and parameter count d
rows.value: The paper gives P(t) ≍ F̂(ϑ(t)) + γK̂pp(ϑ(t)) for the analyzed setting and states that SGD-M has the same scaling laws as SGD. Its reported loss components have power-law scaling, with exponents varying by (α, β) and phase.
rows.locator: Section 3.1, Theorem 3.1 and component scaling table; Sections 4 and G; Appendix K
rows.note: The loss is population risk on PLRF, not held-out language-model cross-entropy. The paper states that the regimes depend on data and target complexity.
rows.check: PLRF is a synthetic quadratic random-features model, not a language model, and the loss is population risk, not held-out LM loss. It does not measure what V1 names. Recorded under fits_no_version.

rows.subject: PLRF (power law random features model)
rows.stage_stated: one-pass stochastic training on synthetic data
rows.operation_detail: Compared DANA-constant and DANA-decaying loss scaling against SGD across model dimensions and training regimes.
rows.measure: Loss exponent under training regimes t = d^ℓ
rows.value: DANA-constant outscales SGD for most tested regimes with 2α > 1; DANA-decaying outscales SGD and DANA-constant for 0 < ℓ < 2α when SGD has not already reached the irreducible-loss level. The paper states DANA performs no worse than SGD elsewhere.
rows.locator: Sections 3 and 4; Figures 1, 5, 6 and 8; Appendix K
rows.note: These are optimizer-dependent loss exponents on the PLRF model, not evidence that every language-model scaling setup follows the same exponents.
rows.check: Compares PLRF loss exponents across optimizers (DANA vs SGD) on a synthetic model, not an LM. Bears on no version; recorded under fits_no_version.

rows.subject: 2-layer LSTMs trained on C4
rows.size_stated: Embedding sizes [16, 24, 32, 48, 64, 96, 128, 192, 256, 512, 1024, 2048, 4096]; hidden dimension is 2 × embedding dimension
rows.operation_detail: Swept LSTM sizes and fit the compute-optimal validation-loss power-law exponent for SGD and DANA-decaying.
rows.measure: Fitted compute-optimal validation-loss exponent versus FLOPs
rows.note: The paper reports these values in Figure 2; it states that κ3 = 0.7 maximizes the compute-optimal loss exponent and outscales SGD. The reported exponents are fitted to validation loss.
rows.check: Correct as recorded. Compute is 6 × non-embedding params × tokens. The paper says the power-law regime holds on intermediate model sizes only, which the row does not note.

rows.subject: 2-layer LSTMs trained on C4
rows.operation_detail: Swept the DANA-decaying momentum learning-rate exponent κ3 and measured validation loss over training tokens.
rows.measure: Validation loss versus training tokens and loss exponent behavior
rows.value: The paper reports that DANA-decaying outscales SGD for 0.6 ≤ κ3 ≤ 0.9.
rows.note: The reported range is a textual summary of the sweep; separate numerical exponents for each κ3 in this range are not given here.
rows.check: Measures how the LSTM compute-optimal loss exponent changes with optimizer schedule, i.e. exponent dependence on training choice (V7). It is not a test of whether loss follows a power law (V1). Per-κ3 exponents appear only in Fig. 21/2c and are not readable from the text.

source_check.correct: DANA-decaying outscales SGD for 0.6 ≤ κ3 ≤ 0.9 on compute-optimal frontiers fitted across embedding sizes 16–192. The embedding-size-128 experiment establishes loss-curve behavior, rather than this compute-optimal exponent result.
source_check.locator_found: Main text, LSTM results; Appendix L.1, Figure 18; Appendix L.2, Figures 21–22.
source_check.problem: The row attaches a scaling result measured across model sizes to the fixed embedding-size-128 experiment.

rows.subject: 2-layer LSTMs trained on C4
rows.operation_detail: Swept the DANA-decaying momentum learning-rate exponent κ3 and measured validation loss over training tokens.
rows.value: The paper reports divergence for DANA-decaying when κ3 < 0.6.
rows.note: This is an intentionally varied optimizer schedule; the result does not imply that ordinary language-model training diverges.
rows.check: Divergence for κ3 < 0.6 is optimizer instability from a deliberately aggressive schedule. It is not evidence against power-law loss scaling. The record's 'reversed' on V1 is wrong.

rows.subject: 2-layer LSTMs trained on C4
rows.operation_detail: Swept the DANA-decaying momentum learning-rate exponent κ3 and measured validation loss over training tokens.
rows.measure: Validation loss and loss exponent behavior
rows.value: The paper reports that DANA-decaying matches SGD when κ3 ≥ 1.0; κ3 = 1.0 is identified as Schedule-Free SGD.
rows.note: The DANA advantage is absent in this tested schedule range.
rows.check: For κ3 ≥ 1.0 (which includes Schedule-Free SGD) the exponent matches SGD. These optimizer choices do not shift the exponent. This is not a V1 result.

source_check.correct: For κ3 ≥ 1.0, compute-optimal exponents fitted across embedding sizes 16–192 return to SGD-like scaling; κ3 = 1.0 corresponds to Schedule-Free SGD and has almost exactly SGD's exponent. Figure 18 separately shows fixed-size loss curves degrading toward SGD.
source_check.locator_found: Appendix L.1, Figure 18; Appendix L.2, Figures 21–22.
source_check.problem: The row conflates fixed-size loss curves with exponent comparisons fitted across model sizes.

rows.subject: PLRF (power law random features model)
rows.size_stated: d varies; numerical compute-optimal comparisons use d = 100 × 2^i, i = 1, …, 15
rows.stage_stated: one-pass stochastic training on synthetic data
rows.operation_detail: Derived and evaluated compute-optimal parameter, loss, and data exponents for SGD, DANA-constant, and DANA-decaying.
rows.measure: Compute-optimal parameter exponent ξ, loss exponent η, and data exponent
rows.value: The paper reports theoretical compute-optimal exponents by phase and states that empirical loss exponents match predictions within 0.09 and parameter exponents within 0.13 across the tested PLRF settings.
rows.uncertainty: Maximum theory–experiment differences stated as 0.09 for loss exponents and 0.132 for parameter exponents
rows.note: The exponents are phase-dependent. Experiments cover 84 (α, β) pairs; the text reports aggregate maximum discrepancies rather than separate rows for each pair.
rows.check: PLRF compute-optimal exponents and their theory–experiment agreement (within 0.09 for loss, 0.13 for parameters). Synthetic model, not an LM, so it does not test V3. Recorded under fits_no_version.

rows.subject: PLRF (power law random features model)
rows.stage_stated: one-pass stochastic training on synthetic data
rows.operation_detail: Compared compute-optimal allocation across optimizer choices.
rows.value: The paper states that DANA-decaying is never compute-optimal with d⋆(f) ≍ f^(1/2) for 2α > 1; its allocation depends on phase. It also states that SGD and DANA can select different compute-optimal tradeoff points.
rows.note: This shows optimizer- and phase-dependent allocation, while the reported laws within phases are still power-law relationships.
rows.check: PLRF result that DANA-decaying's compute-optimal d⋆(f) is never ≍ f^(1/2) for 2α > 1. This is a proxy-model result, not an LM allocation measurement. 'Partial' was also the wrong state; the paper states the result fully. Recorded under fits_no_version.

rows.subject: PLRF (power law random features model)
rows.stage_stated: one-pass stochastic training on synthetic data
rows.operation_detail: Measured fitted scaling exponents using Chinchilla Approach 1 with selected FLOPs windows.

conditions.value: manually adjusted after visual inspection of smoothed loss curves and crossover points

rows.measure: Sensitivity of fitted compute-optimal power-law exponents to the FLOPs fitting window
rows.value: The authors state that changing the FLOPs window can have a dramatic effect on exponent predictions and that they manually adjusted windows because noise made crossover selection difficult.
rows.note: This is an explicit fit-choice sensitivity, not a report of a specific alternative exponent for a different window.
rows.check: Sensitivity of fitted exponents to the FLOPs window, reported for the PLRF experiments only. It is a methodological caveat on synthetic fits. Recorded under fits_no_version.

relationships.condition: 2-layer LSTMs on C4, compute-optimal frontier over intermediate model sizes, SGD and DANA-decaying (κ3 = 0.7).
relationships.reason: Validation loss follows a power law in FLOPs: exponent −0.058 (R² = 0.9997) for SGD and −0.062 (R² = 0.9998) for DANA. All κ3 fits have R² ≥ 0.984 (R3).
relationships.display_finding: Compute exponents were −0.058 for SGD and −0.062 for DANA, with R² of 0.9997 and 0.9998 respectively; all tested κ3 fits achieved R² ≥ 0.984.
